outcomes.title: Past simple irregular verbs
outcomes.objective: Use the correct irregular past simple form to talk about finished events.
prerequisites: Understands that yesterday and last week refer to the past

misconceptions.description: Uses the base form for a finished past event

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses irregular past forms such as went, bought, saw
Does not add -ed to irregular verbs

lesson.title: What I did yesterday
lesson.objective: Describe finished past events with irregular verbs.

objectives: Describe finished past events with irregular verbs.
examples: I went to the market yesterday.
She bought a red hat last week.

items.prompt: Write the past form of 'have': Yesterday I ___ a big lunch.
Write the past form of 'tell': Last night he ___ me a story.

outcomes.studyNotes: Some verbs do not take -ed in the past. They change in a special way and you must learn them. go becomes went, buy becomes bought, see becomes saw. We use these forms for finished events with words like yesterday, last week or two days ago: I went to the market yesterday. She bought a red hat last week. Do not write goed or buyed. Do not use the base form for a finished event: I go to the market yesterday is wrong.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Many common verbs have a special past form. go becomes went, buy becomes bought and see becomes saw. Never add -ed to them.
hints: Is the event finished? Then the verb needs its past form.
Irregular verbs do not end in -ed. Try to remember the special form.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. Learn the special past forms and use them for finished events.

outcomes.objective: Choose a, an or the correctly before singular nouns.
prerequisites: Can tell a vowel sound from a consonant sound

misconceptions.description: Uses a before a vowel sound
Uses a for something already mentioned instead of the
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I met a girl. A girl was friendly.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses the for something already mentioned

lesson.title: Things around me
lesson.objective: Use a, an and the with singular nouns.

objectives: Use a, an and the with singular nouns.
successCriteria: Uses an before a vowel sound
Uses the for the second mention
examples: I have a dog. The dog is brown.
She eats an apple every day.

items.prompt: Write a or an: I see ___ ant on the table.
Write a or the: We have a garden. ___ garden is small.

outcomes.studyNotes: Use a before a consonant sound: a dog, a car. Use an before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u sounds): an apple, an egg. When we mention a thing for the first time we use a or an: I have a dog. When we mention it again, or both people know which one, we use the: The dog is brown. Listen to the sound, not the spelling.

scriptedTutor.explanation: We use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds. We use the when we talk about something already known.
hints: Say the next word aloud. Does it start with a vowel sound?
Was this thing mentioned before? Then use the.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Great. Remember a or an first, then the.

outcomes.title: Comparative adjectives
outcomes.objective: Form and use comparative adjectives with -er or more, followed by than.
prerequisites: Can count syllables in a short word

misconceptions.exampleWrong: Maths is more easier than art.
This film is interestinger than that one.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Adds -er to short adjectives (change y to ier)

lesson.title: Comparing things
lesson.objective: Compare two things with comparative adjectives.

objectives: Compare two things with comparative adjectives.
examples: My brother is taller than me.
This coat is more expensive than that coat.
A mouse is smaller than a cat.

items.prompt: Write the comparative of 'cold': Ice is ___ than water.
Write the comparative of 'popular': Football is ___ than golf.

outcomes.studyNotes: We compare two things with a comparative adjective and than. With short adjectives we add -er: tall, taller; small, smaller. If the adjective ends in -y we change y to ier: happy, happier. With long adjectives (two or more syllables, not ending in -y) we put more before the adjective: expensive, more expensive. Never use both: not more taller. Never add -er to a long adjective.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Short adjectives take -er, long adjectives take more. We never use both and we put than before the second thing.
hints: Is the adjective short or long?
Use either -er or more, not both.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Nice work. Short word -er, long word more.

outcomes.title: Present perfect versus past simple
outcomes.objective: Choose present perfect for unfinished periods and past simple for finished times.
prerequisites: Knows past participles of common verbs

misconceptions.description: Uses present perfect with a finished time marker
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I have bought this jacket yesterday.

misconceptions.description: Uses past simple for a situation that continues now
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I knew my neighbour for ten years (and still do).

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses past simple with finished times (in 2015, last week, ago)
Uses present perfect with for, since, already, yet for unfinished time

lesson.title: Life and time
lesson.objective: Contrast present perfect and past simple.

objectives: Contrast present perfect and past simple.
successCriteria: Present perfect with for and since
examples: I have lived here for five years.

items.prompt: Complete: "She ___ (have) this car since March." Write the verb phrase.
Complete: "We ___ (move) to this street in 2018." Write the verb.

outcomes.studyNotes: We use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time: I lived in Rome in 2010. We often use time words like yesterday, last year, in 2010 or two years ago. We use the present perfect (have or has + past participle) for situations that started in the past and continue now, or for results that matter now. Time words: for, since, already, yet. I have lived here for five years. Never use the present perfect with a finished time word: not I have lived in Rome in 2010.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Finished time word means past simple. A situation that continues to now, with for or since, means present perfect.
hints: Is there a finished time like last week or in 2015?
Does the situation continue until now? Then use have or has plus a participle.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. Finished time is past simple, unfinished time is present perfect.

outcomes.title: Second conditional
outcomes.objective: Form unreal present or future conditionals with if + past simple and would + verb.

misconceptions.description: Uses would in the if clause
misconceptions.exampleWrong: If I would win the lottery, I would buy a boat.

misconceptions.description: Uses present or will in an unreal conditional
misconceptions.exampleWrong: If she knew the answer, she will tell us.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses past simple in the if clause
Uses would + base verb in the result clause

lesson.title: Imagine if
lesson.objective: Talk about imaginary situations with the second conditional.

objectives: Talk about imaginary situations with the second conditional.
examples: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
If she lived nearer, she would walk to school.

items.prompt: Complete: "If I ___ (have) a garden, I would grow flowers." Write the verb.
Complete: "If we lived by the sea, we ___ (swim) daily." Write the verb phrase.

outcomes.studyNotes: We use the second conditional to talk about imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. The if clause uses the past simple, and the result clause uses would plus the base verb: If I had a car, I would drive to work. The past simple here does not talk about the past. With be we often use were for all persons: If I were you, I would wait. Do not use would in the if clause, and do not use will in the result clause.

scriptedTutor.explanation: For imaginary situations, use if plus the past simple, then would plus the base verb in the other part.
hints: Which part is the if clause? It needs a past simple form.
The result part needs would plus a base verb.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Excellent. If plus past, would plus base verb.

outcomes.title: Must, mustn't and don't have to
outcomes.objective: Choose must, mustn't or don't have to to express obligation, prohibition and lack of necessity.
prerequisites: Understands the words forbidden and necessary

misconceptions.description: Thinks mustn't means it is not necessary
misconceptions.exampleWrong: You mustn't bring a pen; the school gives you one.

misconceptions.description: Forms the negative as don't must
misconceptions.exampleWrong: You don't must run in the corridor.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses don't have to for no necessity

successCriteria: don't have to for not necessary
examples: You must wear a seatbelt in a car.
You don't have to pay to enter the park.

items.prompt: Write the modal: In a hospital you ___ shout. It is forbidden.
Write the modal: It is a holiday, so you ___ go to school. It is not necessary.

outcomes.studyNotes: We use must for a strong obligation: You must wear a seatbelt in a car. We use mustn't (must not) when something is forbidden: You mustn't use your phone while driving. We use don't have to when something is not necessary, but it is allowed: You don't have to pay to enter the park. Mustn't and don't have to have very different meanings. Never say don't must.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Must means it is necessary. Mustn't means it is forbidden. Don't have to means it is not necessary.
hints: Is it forbidden, necessary or just not necessary?
Mustn't and don't have to are different.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Great. Forbidden is mustn't, not necessary is don't have to.

outcomes.objective: Choose in, on or at before times, days and months or years.

objectives: Use in, on and at with time words.

items.prompt: Write in, on or at: My train leaves ___ 5 o'clock.

outcomes.studyNotes: Use at with clock times: at 7 o'clock, at noon, at midnight. Use on with days and dates: on Monday, on 5 May. Use in with months, years and seasons: in July, in 2020, in summer. Remember: at for a point in time, on for a day, in for a longer period. Do not say in Monday or at July.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Use at for clock times, on for days and in for months and years.
hints: What kind of time word is it: a clock time, a day or a month?
Clock time uses at, a day uses on, a month or year uses in.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good. At the clock, on the day, in the month.

outcomes.title: Much, many, a few and a little
outcomes.objective: Choose much, many, a few or a little according to countable and uncountable nouns.
prerequisites: Knows common food and people nouns

misconceptions.exampleWrong: There is too many traffic today.

misconceptions.description: Uses a few with uncountable nouns

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses many/a few with countable nouns
Uses much/a little with uncountable nouns

lesson.title: In the kitchen
lesson.objective: Talk about quantities of countable and uncountable things.

objectives: Talk about quantities of countable and uncountable things.
grammar: much, many, a few, a little
examples: How many eggs do we need?

items.prompt: Write much or many: How ___ bottles are there?
Write a few or a little: I have ___ rice left, only a spoonful.

outcomes.studyNotes: Some nouns are countable (eggs, bottles, students) and some are uncountable (rice, water, money, information). With countable plural nouns use many and a few: How many eggs? a few eggs. With uncountable nouns use much and a little: How much rice? a little rice. Much and many are mostly used in questions and negatives. A few and a little mean some, a small number or amount. Do not say many water or a few rice.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Countable plural nouns use many and a few. Uncountable nouns use much and a little.
hints: Can you count the noun with a number?
If you can count it, use many or a few. If not, use much or a little.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the rule again and try once more.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. Count it: many, a few. Cannot count it: much, a little.
